en: The gross body consists of flesh, while the subtle body consists of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Along with the organs of knowledge and action, the intellect and the vital breath reside within that body.
Ignorance is the cause; the witness is consciousness, which illuminates them.
The reflection of consciousness residing in the intellect becomes the agent of merit and demerit.

That very [consciousness] wanders perpetually through the two worlds by the power of karma; therefore, one should distinguish pure awakening from the mere appearance of awakening with extreme effort. (3)
In both waking and dreaming, there is merely a deceptive semblance of consciousness;
however, in deep sleep, when that [semblance] has dissolved, consciousness is pure and reveals its own insentience.
Even during the waking state, the silence of the intellect is illumined by the Pure [Self];
and the functions of the intellect, conjoined with the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), are illumined by consciousness itself. || 5 ||
Just as water heated by fire, being itself possessed of heat, causes heat to the body;
so too the intellect, which is illumined by consciousness, illuminates other objects when it is endowed with their reflections.

The conceptualizations of qualities, defects, and so forth regarding form and other objects are functions residing in the intellect; consciousness is considered to be that which illumines those functions together with their objects.
The consciousness alone is distinct from form, as well as from qualities and defects;
it persists even when there is the conceptualization of forms, tastes, and so forth.
In every moment, the conceptual constructions of the intellect change, but consciousness does not;
consciousness remains within the conceptual constructions of the intellect just as a thread persists among pearls.
Just as a thread covered by pearls is seen in the midst of the pearls,
so too consciousness, though obscured by the fluctuations of mental constructs, is clearly perceived in the interval between two such constructs.
But when the previous conceptual construction has perished, until another arises, non-conceptual consciousness shines forth clearly. (11)
Thus, those who desire the experience of Brahman should diligently practice the cessation of conceptual thought through one, two, or three moments in successive order. (12)
This individual soul is with conceptual construction (savikalpa), whereas that Brahman is without conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka);
this very meaning is expressed by the statement "I am Brahman. (13)
I am the conscious self with conceptualization, while Brahman alone is non-conceptual;
those conceptualizations, which are established by their own nature, must be restrained through diligent effort. (14)

The yogin who is capable [should practice] the samādhi dear to him through the cessation of all [mental activity]; if that is impossible, the faithful one should restrain [the mind] for a moment, [realizing] the Brahman-nature of the self.
One who possesses faith should contemplate one's own state of Brahman through the functions of the intellect;
having understood it according to one's ability by means of the activity of speech, one should practice it constantly with devotion.
The wise know that reflection upon That, discourse about That, mutual awakening to That, and single-minded devotion to That constitute the practice of Brahman. (17)
When the firm realization of the Self as Brahman is attained, just like the [false] notion of the body being the Self, one has accomplished all that was to be done;
at that time, let this person die—he is liberated, there is no doubt about this. (18)

Thus ends the *Laghuvākyavṛtti*, the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
